joint_render.prompt:
Create TWO brand-new, clean, realistic photographs TOGETHER ON ONE near-square 1.05:1 canvas. Layout is a vertical stack: top half is one panoramic 2.10:1 landscape photograph, bottom half is the other panoramic 2.10:1 landscape photograph. Both have exactly the same width and height, touching at a plain straight horizontal seam at EXACTLY 50% canvas height. Full bleed, zero border, no gutter, no text, labels or lettering. They will be cut apart at the seam after generation. Treat as a locked-tripod repeat photograph by a real photographer, one here in autumn, one after five to six months. Render both simultaneously. START THE COMPOSITION FROM SCRATCH. This is a printed field guide, not a poster or advertising. Each photograph has ONE actual mature gardener, the same John from the photos. No posing for camera.

COMPOSITION AND PHYSICAL SCALE take precedence over everything. Make the two compositions register like two exposures from the same tripod: same lens, same sensor crop, same camera elevation and aim, same focus distance, same ground plane, same fixed architectural features at precisely corresponding positions in both individual frames. No zoom or camera move. Imagine marking his standing spot with chalk: both times John's two boots are on the same right-hand strip of turf, at the same distance from the camera and close to the nearest right-hand corner of the bed. His head, hands, boots and shoulders are demonstrably the SAME ABSOLUTE PHYSICAL SIZE when one printed photograph is laid over the other. In particular his face and skull must be the SAME WIDTH in pixels in both images, and his boots the same heel-to-toe length. Do NOT make the spring gardener a little background figure or enlarge the autumn gardener to fill the top frame. Do not zoom in on the autumn action. Set up the framing around the SPRING working pose first with head-to-shoes fitting and a little headroom, then use that exact roomier composition for AUTUMN; let the top of his lowered autumn head naturally sit a little lower in the picture. A useful cue: the same nearby house brick is the same size in both images, and John's skull is roughly a brick long from front to back in BOTH. Both times John is presented near side-on in a three-quarter working profile looking left and down, so face width, nose, soft receding chin, short grey beard and build are directly comparable. Use genuinely photographed human anatomy. Face portrait board = real identity, second board = his two actual clothes.

Home garden in Cornwall: weathered pale timber panel fence on low moss-marked grey/buff masonry, two distinct upright fence posts (roughly 12% and 57% across each panorama), just a thin sliver of the glass/aluminium greenhouse sitting on pale grey brick base at extreme right, barely 6–8% of width. Use third reference's site details for materials only. No blue shed, other beds, sky, extra objects, or paths. Dense convincing mown green lawn with occasional clover. Across the nearer left and central ground lies a modest rectangle about 1.2 x 1.8 metres. Same four corners in the same places in both panels. The rear edge spans the bay of those two fixed posts, parallel to the low wall with a narrow 15–20cm grass strip behind it. The long front edge can be seen above the foreground grass border; right edge falls beside John's boots. A level camera from a slight downward three-quarter viewing angle makes the teaching detail clear while capturing enough of the man. Give the action, the ground and the man's body realistic relative sizes. Prioritize believable spontaneous photography, fine skin, fabric and grass texture.

TOP / LATE AUTUMN: John wears plain charcoal crewneck jumper, blue jeans and brown work shoes from the real first outfit. Cool damp overcast daylight, some muted autumn colour. Show the opaque dark bottle-green tarp lying flush directly on the entire cut-back patch, irregularly weighted at its edges with ordinary old bricks and a couple of stones. John on the right at the SAME DEPTH AS BELOW carries the final old brick down towards its visible place at the near right hem. Catch him midway through a natural side-on bend / hip hinge with softly bent knees, brick visibly in his hand descending towards the hem, gaze on the task. It is fine if the brick still has a little way to travel; this allows for a moderate forward bend rather than kneeling close to the lens. His upper arm, hands and head belong in the same real-world scale as the spring adult. Do not pull the camera closer or make his face a closeup.

BOTTOM / LATE SPRING: Same exact rectangle directly below the four outside corners of the tarp above, now uncovered. Folded tarp and weights lie on green grass off its rear RIGHT corner, not pushing or hiding the bed. John, now wearing the real faded olive short-sleeve T-shirt and olive work shorts, bare forearms and calves, brown shoes, is at the SAME working spot, working side-on with a mild hip hinge, relaxed shoulders and comfortable stance, feet fairly close together. A mild sunny spring day, natural cast shadows. He draws a light stroke with a modest 30 cm wide rigid steel soil rake, a straight shaft ending in a metal socket fixed at the EXACT CENTRE OF THE CROSSBAR, visually equal-length left and right halves, regular teeth contacting the turf. Hands lightly spaced along a single wooden handle. At the teeth a little ragged lip of fine dead lawn fibres and a few attached weed runners rises out of the same layer that covers the ground. Low matted grey-brown dead lawn, patchy compact damp soil showing through, a short darker combed swathe. No piled weeds, no isolated intact loose weed plants, no hay. Short lush live grass is outside the rectangle. Undramatic natural colour; keep face, hands, rake head, brick and patch legible at book size. Finish as the single precisely halved canvas of two matched panoramas.

verification_notes: At native resolution, the visible skulls are both approximately 90 pixels across. The visible boot size and fence post positions agree. The front corners of the exposed patch follow the sheet corners to about 15 pixels. Manual image estimates, not measured physical dimensions.

visual_research.source: University of Minnesota Turfgrass Science, Gary Deters, Figure 3
visual_research.observation: Direct lawn example after removing an opaque tarp: bare ground mixed with brown vegetation in irregular low patches. Some violets survived in this trial.

visual_research.source: Winterizing Garden Beds, Tarping to Reduce Tillage, p. 8
visual_research.observation: Three-frame bed sequence showing brown residual growth and exposed soil as the cover is pulled back.
